entry.title: SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2: How SAP Is Rebuilding the Future of Customer Experience
entry.content:
SAP has quietly reset the clock on its CRM platform. SAP Sales Cloud Version 2 (V2) isn't a facelift or a routine upgrade —

Transition to V2

SAP's CRM story stretches back decades — from the original WebUI, through ABAP-based CRM On-Premise, into Cloud for Customer (C4C), and eventually Sales Cloud V1. V2 is SAP's answer to all of that history: a microservices architecture, zero-downtime quarterly releases, and a clean OData V4 API layer that fully replaces the older OData V2 foundation V1 was built on.

 

A Sales Process Built Around the Rep, Not the System

Before diving into individual apps, it's worth understanding how V2 reshapes the day-to-day sales workflow itself.

The Digital Sales Workplace: A Command Center for Reps

At the center of Sales Cloud V2 sits the Digital Sales Workplace — essentially a daily command center purpose-built for sales reps. It pulls together everything a salesperson touches in a day, from prepping for calls to tracking how deals are progressing, all in one place.

The main screen combines a prioritized to-do list, an integrated calendar, and one-click access to the tools reps rely on most: call lists, tasks, opportunities, leads, emails, and the sales navigator.

That consolidation translates into speed. Reps can create accounts, contacts, tasks, appointments, leads, opportunities, and quotes — or log a call — without ever leaving the dashboard. A Kanban-style pipeline view rounds it out, letting reps drag and drop deals across stages so pipeline progress is always visible at a glance.

A Seamless Path From Lead to Quote

Consistency is what makes a sales process scalable, and V2 bakes that consistency in through a connected chain of applications that carry a deal from first contact to close. The standard flow runs through four stages:

Lead → Opportunity → Quote → Sales Order

1. Lead capture

Everything starts in the Leads app, where reps view and manage every incoming lead. Each record carries the details that matter — source (website form, event, referral), contact information, engagement history, lead score, and follow-up status — so reps can quickly judge lead quality and act: schedule a call, hand it off to a teammate, or convert it straight into an opportunity.

2. Opportunity management

Once qualified, a lead becomes an opportunity and moves into the Opportunities app, where a Kanban-style board tracks its progress across pipeline stages. From here, reps can:

  • Drag opportunities from one stage to the next (say, from "Qualification" to "Proposal")
  • Schedule follow-ups
  • Send emails without leaving the workspace
  • Book meetings or site visits
  • Log call notes and meeting summaries

3. Quote creation

When an opportunity matures, the Quotes app takes over. Here, users generate customer-specific proposals, adjust pricing and discounts, apply terms and conditions, and track the deal through its approval workflow.

4. Sales order generation

Once a quote is approved, native integration with SAP S/4HANA (or other back-end systems) converts it directly into a Sales Order — no manual re-entry required.

Turning Data Into Decisions: Analytics in V2

Good decisions start with visibility, and analytics sits at the core of how Sales Cloud V2 helps teams stay ahead of performance rather than reacting to it.

Pipeline Manager (Bubble Chart View) gives the pipeline a visual, intuitive shape: every deal appears as a bubble, sized by potential value and colored by urgency, so reps and managers can spot the opportunities that deserve attention first.

Forecast Tracker brings real-time and predictive forecasting into a single view. From here, sales managers can set and adjust forecast targets, compare actual performance against what was forecasted, and monitor trends over time.

Beyond what's built in, Predefined and Custom Reports extend the picture — standard reporting covers leads, opportunities, and sales performance, while integration with SAP Analytics Cloud opens the door to deeper, custom dashboards tailored to specific business needs.

Where AI Actually Shows Up in the Workflow

Sales Cloud V2 doesn't bolt AI on as an afterthought — it's woven through the tools reps and managers use every day.

Lead and opportunity scoring ranks each lead and opportunity using past engagement, deal history, and predictive signals, so it's immediately clear which ones are most likely to close and deserve priority in the pipeline.

Email draft recommender writes personalized email drafts in seconds. Reps can dial in the tone — formal or friendly — and the length, sending faster without starting each message from a blank page.

AI-driven recommendations step in when the next move isn't obvious. The system suggests concrete next steps — schedule a follow-up call, send a quote, offer a discount — based on what's worked in similar deals before, and it even flags upsell opportunities based on past buying behavior.

Account synopsis distills a customer account into a short, clear summary: recent activity, past purchases, open challenges, and overall sales potential, all in a single snapshot.

Predictive analytics takes reporting a step further. Tools like the Pipeline Bubble Chart and Forecast Tracker use AI to project deal outcomes, flagging high-potential and at-risk opportunities and checking real-time results against forecasts — so teams can act early rather than after the fact.

Joule, SAP's AI agent, ties it all together as a conversational assistant. Ask it something like "Which opportunities are at risk this quarter?" or "What's the forecast for Q3?" and it answers in real time, grounded in your own company's data.

The Big Q1 2026 Story: Joule Studio Goes GA

If there's one headline from this release cycle, it's this: Joule Studio reached General Availability in Q1 2026 — the single biggest development in Sales Cloud V2 since it launched. It's the shift SAP has been signaling since Sapphire 2025: moving Joule from a reactive AI copilot into a proactive agent-building platform.

What Actually Changed

Before Joule Studio, Joule behaved like a copilot — you asked, it answered. Joule Studio changes that relationship entirely by letting you build custom AI agents that run multi-step workflows on their own. These agents connect Sales Cloud V2, S/4HANA, third-party systems, and external data sources into a single automated flow, with no extra tooling and no manual handoffs in between.

💡What that looks like in practice: An agent keeps watch over all open Q2 opportunities. If a deal hasn't had customer contact in 14 days and is set to close this quarter, the agent automatically drafts a follow-up email, logs the activity, and alerts the account manager — no one had to ask it to

To go deeper on building and configuring these agents:

  • Joule Studio — Build AI Agents, Apps, and Workflows
  • What is Joule Studio? — SAP Help Portal
  • Joule Setup for SAP Sales Cloud Version 2

The recommended path: start with core Joule capabilities, configure onboarding and permissions, and only then move on to designing custom agents and workflows around your own business processes.

Sales Intelligence: Scoring Deals on What Actually Happens

Q1 2026 also marked the first real leap forward in deal intelligence. Rather than relying on AI guesswork, the system now watches engagement patterns at the deal level and surfaces risk signals grounded in historical deal-slippage data — patterns pulled from real outcomes, not assumptions.

A few resources worth bookmarking on this:

Opportunity Scoring (Deal Intelligence) — SAP Help Portal. Covers overview screens showing the opportunity score, the factors influencing it, and the underlying scoring concepts. Read it here

View Deal Scoring Predictions — SAP Help Portal. The best source for screenshots of the opportunity score UI, the score popup, the insights panel, the score trend, and the risk explanation view

 

 

SAP Sales Cloud V2 — Deal Intelligence Overview. A broader product walkthrough covering opportunity scoring and pipeline acceleration. Read it here

Guided selling ties this all together, giving reps account insights and timelines, relationship intelligence, and prescriptive next-best-action recommendations — while reinforcing good selling habits through embedded gamification

Pipeline Manager Visualization shows exactly how Deal Intelligence surfaces inside pipeline charts and opportunity views, blending the bubble chart with score visualization.

Analytics, Rebuilt From the Ground Up

Q1 2026's analytics update went beyond dashboards. Redesigned forecasting views now support multi-level drill-down, and V2's analytics layer introduces intent-based navigation — the ability to jump from an embedded SAC story straight to the exact CRM record you need to review or update, in just two clicks.

The December 2025 release laid the groundwork for this: it added currency conversion for amount-based attributes inside embedded SAC stories, along with a live connection to Enterprise SAC that keeps data in the source system and discards it once the story closes — a meaningful step forward for data security.

Release History: What's Landed So Far

Q1 2026 — Joule Studio GA + Deal Intelligence + Forecasting Rebuild

The custom AI agent builder goes generally available, joined by activity-based risk scoring, multi-level forecast drill-down, and improvements to mobile and CTI.

December 2025 — Enterprise SAC Live Connection + Currency Conversion

A real-time live connection to Enterprise SAP Analytics Cloud, plus currency conversion support for global reporting inside embedded SAC stories.

2508 — WalkMe Integration + Migration & Adoption Improvements

This release focused squarely on adoption, onboarding, and transition support across both Sales and Service Cloud. Highlights included:

  • WalkMe integration for guided in-app user journeys
  • Smart content flows for feature discovery and onboarding
  • An improved Readiness Check and better Data Transfer tooling
  • Stronger support for V1 → V2 transition planning

2508 — Opportunity Management & Guided Selling Enhancements

Sales execution kept evolving with sharper opportunity management and guidance experiences:

  • Enhancements to Opportunity Management
  • Improved Guided Selling scenarios
  • Better opportunity execution support
  • A more productive seller workspace experience

2508 — Service Operations & Integration Improvements

Service teams saw updates aimed at operational efficiency and more connected experiences:

  • Ticket management enhancements
  • Integration improvements across service processes
  • Faster navigation and execution
  • Improved visibility into service operations

Q1 2026 — Joule Studio GA + Deal Intelligence + Forecasting Rebuild

Custom AI agent capabilities went generally available alongside deeper built-in intelligence:

  • Build and manage custom AI agents with Joule Studio
  • Activity-based opportunity risk scoring
  • Forecast drill-down with improved analytics
  • Mobile and CTI enhancements

December 2025 — Enterprise SAC Live Connection

Analytics became more scalable across global organizations:

  • Live connection to Enterprise SAP Analytics Cloud
  • Reduced duplication of analytical data

More secure reporting experiences

Q3 2025 — Business Information Extraction Extended to Cases

AI capabilities expanded into service execution:

  • Automatic extraction of business entities from customer interactions
  • Smarter case categorization
  • ML-generated interaction summaries
  • Resolution insights paired with sentiment awareness

September 2025 — Intent-Based Navigation in Analytics

Analytics moved from pure reporting toward action-oriented workflows:

  • Direct navigation from analytics to CRM business objects
  • Faster movement from insight to execution
  • Reduced context switching
  • Improved operational productivity

Where This Is All Heading

Across SAP Customer Experience, the innovation roadmap keeps circling back to three themes:

  • Sales → Intelligent Revenue Execution
  • Service → AI-Assisted Resolution
  • ESM → Connected Enterprise Service Delivery

For more release detail and screenshots, see the SAP Sales and Service Cloud 2508 Release Briefing.

The takeaway: SAP Sales Cloud V2 isn't just an incremental release cycle — it's a platform that's actively becoming more autonomous, more predictive, and more integrated with every quarter. For teams starting fresh, V2 is the clear starting point.

entry.title: Omnichannel Commerce & B2B Digital Transformation with the Advanced Success Plan for SAP CX
entry.content:
Connected by Design: Operationalizing Omnichannel Commerce & B2B Transformation with the Advanced Success Plan for SAP Customer Experience

 Modern B2B buyers expect seamless experiences across web, mobile, marketplaces, and partner portals. In fact, 84% of B2B buyers say it is important for suppliers to operate across multiple online and offline channels [Digital Commerce 360, 2025].

To meet these expectations, organizations must move beyond siloed commerce channels toward a connected autonomous CX model that integrates commerce, order sourcing, fulfilment, and customer support across the full customer journey.

The Advanced Success Plan for SAP Customer Experience supports this shift by accelerating omnichannel capability build-out through outcome-based governance. It helps organizations move from fragmented execution to coordinated operations—enabling consistent cross-channel experiences, aligning commerce with sales and service execution, and improving conversion and repeat purchase through end-to-end alignment.

The Reality of B2B Buying

B2B buying is rarely linear anymore. Buyers often switch between digital channels, sales teams, and service touchpoints before deciding. Research from McKinsey’s B2B Pulse highlights that buyers typically engage across multiple interaction channels before making a decision [McKinsey, 2021].

This reflects how digital commerce has become a core part of the buying process, with 58% of global B2B retailers selling on at least three e-commerce platforms [DHL, 2025].

At the same time, expectations have shifted. Consistency across channels is assumed, digital self-service is often the starting point, and speed and transparency are baseline requirements.

That creates a dual challenge for organizations: improving customer experience while also managing increasing operational complexity behind the scenes.

Convergence of Commerce, Sales, and Service

B2B environments combine complex operations with tightly connected customer journeys. Organizations must manage customer-specific pricing and contracts, large and dynamic product catalogs, multi-step approvals, distributed fulfilment models, and integrations across commerce, ERP, sales, and service systems.

Customers, however, do not see this complexity. They experience a single journey, from discovery to purchase, fulfilment, and support, and expect it to feel seamless.

A typical journey may include discovering products online, aligning pricing with sales, placing orders through self-service channels, and resolving issues via service interactions. Expectations for real-time visibility, fast issue resolution, and consistent engagement continue to rise, as highlighted in research such as DHL’s B2B E-Commerce Trends [DHL, 2025].

The same DHL report also shows that 78% of B2B retailers expect website sales to grow over the next three to five years, which reinforces how central digital channels have become [DHL, 2025].

Yet many organizations still operate in silos. The result is often inconsistent data, limited visibility across interactions, slower issue resolution, and disconnected customer experiences. This is why omnichannel transformation is not about adding channels, but about connecting commerce, sales, and service into a unified operating flow.

Process Excellence as a Foundation

As complexity increases, end-to-end process alignment becomes critical. Customers experience outcomes, not systems, and those outcomes depend on how well processes are connected across commerce, sales, service, and fulfilment.

Breakdowns typically occur when sales agreements are not reflected in commerce systems, fulfilment is not aligned with order promises, service teams lack customer context, or data differs across channels. These are not isolated system issues, but symptoms of disconnected processes.

In practice, that can mean a customer sees one price in the portal, a different one in the quote, and another one in the order confirmation. It can also mean service teams have to ask customers to repeat information that already exists elsewhere in the organization. Even when the underlying technology is in place, the experience still feels broken if the process is not connected.

Organizations that invest in process excellence are better positioned to deliver consistent experiences, reduce friction, improve operational efficiency, and scale complex B2B models. Process alignment also makes it easier to respond to change, because teams can adapt faster when the underlying journey is not held together by disconnected handoffs.

 Why Omnichannel Matters

Omnichannel in B2B is not just about offering more ways to buy. It is about making those ways work together. When the customer starts on one channel and finishes on another, the handoff needs to feel natural. If not, the customer experience becomes fragmented very quickly.

That matters because B2B buyers are increasingly comparing their business purchasing experience to the consumer experiences they already know. They expect simple navigation, transparent pricing, reliable order updates, and a service team that understands the full context of the account. In other words, they want the convenience of digital commerce without losing the support and complexity that B2B purchasing often requires.

This is also where many companies struggle. They may have a strong storefront, but weak back-end coordination. Or they may have good sales support, but poor visibility once the order has been placed. Omnichannel transformation closes that gap by connecting the customer-facing experience with the operational processes behind it.

Accelerating Outcomes with the Advanced Success Plan for SAP Customer Experience

The Advanced Success Plan for SAP Customer Experience helps organizations accelerate omnichannel capability build-out through outcome-based governance and alignment between strategy and execution.

Rather than focusing only on implementation, the emphasis is on measurable outcomes across the full customer journey. This includes enabling consistent omnichannel experiences, aligning SAP Commerce Cloud, SAP Sales and Service Cloud, and fulfilment processes, managing catalog and contract complexity at scale, improving order sourcing and fulfilment coordination, and strengthening end-to-end process alignment.

The goal is to ensure all capabilities operate as one connected system rather than separate functions.

That becomes especially important in B2B environments where a single transaction can involve multiple stakeholders, custom pricing rules, approval steps, and several systems working together at once. Without clear governance and alignment, even well-designed digital tools can create confusion instead of clarity.

With the right operating model, however, organizations can turn complexity into a strength. They can reduce friction for customers, improve efficiency internally, and create a more reliable buying experience across every channel.

The Advanced Success Plan for SAP Customer Experience includes access to Business Process Best Practices which helps customers understand the end-to-end process flow and best practices for executing business processes across SAP Sales and Service. This service showcases reference processes and bridges the gaps that can occur during rapid implementations of solutions in complex landscapes or when implementation of multiple solutions creates fragmented processes without taking into consideration unique end-to-end view.

 

Conclusion

Omnichannel commerce and B2B digital transformation are reshaping how organizations engage customers and deliver value. Success depends on connecting commerce, sales, service, and fulfilment into a unified operating model supported by strong end-to-end processes.

Organizations that focus on process excellence and outcome-based governance are better positioned to scale effectively and meet rising customer expectations. The Advanced Success Plan for SAP Customer Experience enables this by connecting strategy to execution and supporting consistent outcomes across the customer journey.

For B2B companies, the real shift is not just digital adoption. It is building a model where channels, processes, and teams work together in a way that feels simple to the customer, even when the operation behind it is complex.

entry.title: V1-V2 Transition: A Consultant's Playbook — Part 1: Know Before You Go (The Pre-Assessment)
entry.content:
V1-V2 Transition: A Consultant's Playbook
— Part 1: Know Before You Go (The Pre-Assessment)

This is Part 1 of a multi-part series on planning and executing a phased SAP Sales & Service Cloud V1-to-V2 transition. Part 2 covers the Lite Assessment, and Part 3 will cover execution.

I want to start with a disclaimer: this is not an official SAP best-practice guide. There are plenty of those already, and they're worth reading. What I want to share instead is how I actually run the preparation phase of a V1-to-V2 transition on the ground, with real customers, based on my own personal experience as a consultant the decisions I make, the tools I lean on, and the reasoning behind them.

If you're a customer, partner, or fellow SAP consultant standing at the start of a phased migration, my hope is that this gives you a practical mental model of what "preparation" really means before you touch a single configuration setting.

Why Preparation Is the Phase That Decides Everything

A phased migration lives or dies on how well you understand the starting point. Before I ever talk about timelines, resourcing, or go-live waves, I need to answer three questions for myself: How big is this really? How customized is the current system? And where does the customer's process actually deviate from SAP standard and why?

I answer these questions in stages, through assessment types that build on each other: the Pre-Assessment, which this post is about, and the Lite Assessment, which gets its own post next. (There's also a Deep Assessment, but that's a topic for another day — this series focuses on getting the scope and direction right before you commit real effort.)

Worth knowing up front: these aren't just internal steps I run informally they're actual SAP services that a customer can book through SAP. The Pre-Assessment is free of charge. The Lite Assessment and the Deep Assessment, on the other hand, are paid services. That distinction matters for how a customer plans their transition budget, and it's part of why the Pre-Assessment is scoped the way it is. It's meant to be a low-commitment first step before anyone spends money on a deeper assessment.

If you're a customer reading this and any of it sounds relevant to your own situation, these services can be requested directly through your SAP contact person you don't need a project already underway to ask about a Pre-Assessment. I've personally run all three assessment types many times, and not only directly between SAP and a customer. Quite often in a constellation where an SAP partner is involved alongside the customer, with me supporting as the SAP-side consultant.

One more scoping note: some SAP partners have built their own CRM migration assessment methodologies, and those are worth looking into as well. This series isn't about comparing approaches. My focus here is specifically the V1-to-V2 transition path as I run it as an SAP consultant. My hope is simply to give a genuine, detailed look into that path, in case it helps someone else shape their own.

The Pre-Assessment: A Feature Parity Check, Not an Effort Estimate

The Pre-Assessment is deliberately lightweight, and it has a narrower job than people sometimes expect. At this stage I'm not yet trying to size effort or estimate redesign work, I'm answering one question: can this customer move to V2 today, and if not, what's blocking them? In other words, it's a feature parity check and a showstopper hunt, not a full effort assessment. It typically runs about two weeks, start to finish. Anything that requires an AI-powered code analysis, like AssessMate, comes later — that only enters the picture once we're past the "can we even go" question and into the "how much work is it" question during the Lite Assessment.

The Discovery Questionnaire

Several colleagues and I built this internally, based on shared experience across many V1-to-V2 transition projects. It's not a single generic form it's a structured workbook with a few tabs that build on each other:

  • Basic Questions — landscape-level questions: standalone vs. integrated with a backend ERP or S/4HANA system, industry solutions in use, analytical tools (SAP BI, SAC, or third-party), other SAP or non-SAP integrations, how many custom namespaces exist, how long the system has been running and its data volume, existing business pain points, and — usefully — whether the customer is even comfortable with a phased deployment in the first place.
  • Process Areas — every relevant process area (Account & Contacts, Products, Lead Management, Opportunity Management, Ticket Management, and so on) gets marked as in use or not, together with a rough level of customization. This is the first complexity signal I get — before I've looked at a single detailed capability question, I already have a sense of where the customization pressure in this account sits, and this early signal is one of the inputs I carry forward into the T-shirt size effort estimation once I get to the Lite Assessment.
  • Process Area Questions — this is where it gets granular. For every capability within an in-use process area, the sheet captures the information source, my own expert review and comments, and then the customer's review and response for validation. It also derives whether the feature is available in V2 today, what the roadmap timeline looks like if not, and a resulting parity status.
  • Dashboard — aggregates parity status by process area into charts I take straight into the final presentation.

SAP Sales & Service Cloud Transformation PreAssessment Questionaire


How the Readiness Check Feeds the Questionnaire

One detail that tends to surprise people: a large part of the Pre-Assessment happens without a single live customer interaction. In many cases, the customer simply exports the Readiness Check report from their own C4C system and sends it to me as an Excel file by email. I use that export as the information source for the Process Area Questions tab and fill in my expert review based on it — the customer doesn't need to answer anything yet at this point.

Only the questions that are genuinely still open after that, things the Readiness Check export can't answer on its own, I go back to the customer, either in a short call or by email, and get captured in the Customer Review and Customer Response columns. That keeps the customer's time investment small and reserves live interaction for the questions that actually need their input.

SAP Sales & Service Cloud Transformation PreAssessment Questionaire: Process Area


From Dashboard to Final Presentation

Once every open question is answered, I don't build a separate deck from scratch — I go straight to the questionnaire's Dashboard tab. It aggregates parity status per process area (available in V2, available and already in use, or not available in V2 but used in V1) into a chart, and that chart goes directly into the final Pre-Assessment presentation as the "assessment results" overview.

SAP Sales & Service Cloud Transformation PreAssessment Questionaire: Dashboard

But I don't stop at one aggregate chart. The executive summary slide up front sorts everything into three buckets, and I've found this is what customers actually remember from the whole session:

  • Process parity — the process areas that transition cleanly, with no material gap
  • Objects on the roadmap — capabilities not available in V2 today, each one tagged with the quarter it's expected to land in, based on the public product roadmap
  • Objects with extended feature coverage — the objects that carry customer-specific extensions and will need a closer look later

Executive summary

 

For every process area, I also break the aggregate chart down into its own slide with a small "Findings" box next to it. That's where the roadmap-tagged gaps live — for example, a duplicate-check capability that isn't available yet but is scheduled for a specific quarter — and it's also where I flag things that aren't feature gaps at all but genuine platform limits worth knowing early, like a channel or volume limit that only matters if the customer's setup happens to exceed it.

Pre-Assessment: Process area detail slide – chart with findings callout



Where this gets more than just a chart-copy exercise is with anything that comes out as not available in V2 but used in V1. For every one of those, I make it a point to actually show the gap, not just name it — either a screenshot of the V1 feature in question, or, ideally, a short live demo during the presentation itself. Then I check the public SAP product roadmap for that capability and tell the customer, as concretely as I can, whether and when it's expected to land in V2. That combination — showing the gap and pairing it with a roadmap-based timing answer — is what turns a raw parity chart into something the customer can actually plan around.

I also dedicate a slide to configuration and administration items that sit outside the process-area charts entirely — things like mashups that need rebuilding, language adaptations that need reconfiguring, integrations that need re-establishing, and reporting content that doesn't migrate automatically. None of that shows up in a parity chart built around business objects, but it belongs in the same conversation, because it affects the same go-live timeline.

Finally, I close with a short, forward-looking slide on customer-specific extensions  how many PDI solutions exist, roughly how many objects and fields carry extensions without going into effort or complexity yet. That's a deliberate handoff: it tells the customer what's coming, without answering it here. The Pre-Assessment presentation itself ends with a small set of concrete recommendations  build V2 know-how internally, start planning the Lite or Deep Assessment, review existing extensions, evaluate integration needs, and consider a proof of concept rather than a vague "let's talk next steps."

By the end of the Pre-Assessment, I have two things: a clear answer on feature parity including any showstoppers that push parts of the timeline out, backed by an actual roadmap date rather than a guess and a customer who now understands, concretely, why a migration date might need to move rather than just being told "it depends." The whole exercise, questionnaire through final presentation, typically takes about two weeks deliberately short, because its job is to answer "can we go," not "how do we go."

A Second Outcome: An Early Read on Landscape Complexity

Feature parity isn't the only thing the Pre-Assessment leaves me with. Alongside the Discovery Questionnaire, I also pull up the official Readiness Check tool directly in the customer's system — and its PDI Solutions tab gives me an independent, tool-generated complexity signal that's worth calling out on its own.

For every PDI solution in the system, this tab lists the product ID, a description, a calculated complexity percentage, and a transition status (Supported, Currently Not Supported, or Not Supported). I don't need AssessMate or a Lite Assessment workshop to get this — it's right there in the Readiness Check tool, based purely on what's actually deployed.

Readiness Check tool – PDI Solutions tab with complexity % and transition status



Even at a glance, this tells me something useful: how many PDI solutions exist at all, and roughly how transferable each one looks out of the box. A landscape with twenty-plus PDI solutions, most flagged "Not Supported," tells a very different story than one with two or three simple ones — and that story belongs in the Pre-Assessment presentation just as much as the feature parity chart does. It's also one more thread I carry forward: alongside the questionnaire's customization signal, it helps me set expectations for how substantial the Lite or Deep Assessment conversation is likely to be before we've even scheduled it.

What's Next

The Pre-Assessment tells us whether we can go and roughly what's still missing. It doesn't tell us how much work the customer's specific customizations will actually take, or why those customizations exist in the first place — that's the job of the Lite Assessment, and it's where things get genuinely hands-on.

In Part 2, I'll walk through how AssessMate supports the Lite Assessment, how I plan the workshops, and why business process deep dives with actual end users are the part of this whole exercise I'd never let get cut for time. ("V1-V2 Transition: A Consultant's Playbook — Part 2: Getting Into the Weeds (The Lite Assessment)" )

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This post reflects my personal approach and experience as a consultant, and does not represent official SAP guidance. Feedback and differing perspectives are very welcome in the comments.

entry.title: A Beginner's Guide to Custom Approval Workflows in SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2 Using SAP BPA
entry.content:
Building custom approval processes in SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 is not a lift-and-shift from V1. It needs to be rebuilt from scratch using SAP Build Process Automation. If you are not sure where to start, this guide walks you through the foundational steps and key concepts to get you going.

What You Need to Know First

Understanding Approval Processes

An approval process is a structured workflow in which a record or transaction (such as a sales quote, expense claim) must be reviewed and formally approved by one or more designated individuals before it can be acted upon or progressed. Organisations typically need approval processes to enforce governance, ensure accountability, and manage risk. For example, requiring managerial sign-off whenever a deal value exceeds a threshold, or ensuring that high-impact records are not processed without proper oversight.

In SAP Sales and Service Cloud V1, a standard approval framework is available out of the box and can be configured natively for supported standard business objects. For custom business objects (those built using SAP Cloud Applications Studio- the SDK-based development environment for V1), developers can extend and leverage this same standard approval framework programmatically, allowing custom objects to participate in the same approval lifecycle as standard ones. Approvers in V1 can receive notifications and act on approval tasks like approving or rejecting records, directly within the SAP Sales and Service Cloud V1 application itself.

In SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2, standard business objects that support approvals out of the box continue to allow notifications, approvals, and rejections to be handled natively within the V2 application. However, the V1 approval configurations do not migrate automatically to V2, and the underlying approval framework has changed significantly. For custom business objects, or standard objects where a built-in approval process is not available out of the box, the recommended approach is to integrate with SAP Build Process Automation (BPA) - a low-code workflow tool on SAP BTP. When approvals are routed through SAP BPA, approvers do not receive or act on tasks within SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 directly. Instead, they access their approval tasks via SAP Task Center or SAP BPA My Inbox, without needing direct access to the V2 application.

What are we doing?

Consider a scenario where a custom Business Object (e.g., a Cost Estimate) in SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 requires managerial approval whenever the amount on the instance exceeds ₹2,000. When an employee creates and saves such a BO instance, the system should automatically route an approval request to the responsible employee's manager. The manager should be able to review the record and approve or reject it.

How is this realised in V2?

In V2, the recommended way to implement such a custom approval process is through integration with SAP Build Process Automation (BPA). When the business object instance is saved and meets the approval condition, V2 triggers an approval workflow in SAP BPA, which routes the task to the responsible manager. The manager receives the approval task in SAP BPA My Inbox or SAP Task Center and can approve or reject the request from there.

Why are we doing this?

SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 does not carry over approval processes from V1 automatically - you need to rebuild them, and SAP BPA is the recommended tool to do this. This is relevant for two groups of customers:

  • Those migrating from SAP Sales and Service Cloud V1 to V2, who need to rebuild their existing approval processes in the new environment.
  • Those who need to create a custom approval process - either for Custom Business Objects built using Side-by-Side Extensibility (custom BOs hosted on SAP BTP, outside the core V2 system), or for standard Business Objects for which the standard approval process is not available out of the box.

What is SAP Build Process Automation (BPA)?

Think of SAP BPA as a ‘workflow builder’ - a low-code/no-code tool on SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) that lets you design, automate, and manage approval processes without writing complex code. Instead of approvals being handled manually or inside the old V1 system, BPA acts as the 'engine' that drives who approves what, when, and how.

Key Terms You Will Encounter:

Term

Plain English Meaning

Business Object (BO)

A record in the system - for example, a Sales Quote or a Custom BO Instance

Decision Table

A simple table (like Excel) where you define rules: 'IF this condition, THEN do that'
Ex: IF Amount <2500 THEN Direct Manager
        IF Amount >2500 THEN Senior Manager

API Trigger

The 'start button' for your workflow - an external system sends a signal to kick off the approval process

Action

A call to an external system (e.g., to fetch an approver or update a record)

Environment

A deployment space in BPA - think of it like a 'folder' where your live workflows run

Destination

A saved connection in BTP that tells BPA how to reach an external system or API

API Key

A password-like token that allows an external system to trigger your BPA workflow securely

Service Key

Credential used to authenticate API calls to BPA

Workflow Instance ID

A unique ID generated each time a workflow is triggered - like a ticket number for that specific approval run

Task ID

The ID of the specific approval task within a running workflow

Why this matters?

SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 supports integration with SAP BPA to manage approval workflows - particularly for process steps in process management. This integration allows external stakeholders to access approval tasks from SAP Task Center without needing direct access to SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 itself. This is an important distinction from V1- In V2, approvals driven by SAP BPA are not actioned inside the V2 application - the approver's entry point is Task Center or BPA My Inbox.

Getting Started: Prerequisites Before You Build Your Approval Workflow

Before building your approval workflow, there are a few foundational components that need to be configured. These prerequisites ensure that SAP Build Process Automation can communicate with external systems, authenticate API calls, and execute workflow actions successfully.

  • Step 1: Create an Environment in SAP Build Lobby
  • Step 2: Create BTP Destinations
  • Step 3: Add BTP Destinations to SAP BPA
  • Step 4: Create a Service Key in BTP
  • Step 5: Create an API Key
  • Step 6: Create an Action Project

With the prerequisites outlined, let's dive into each of them.

Step 1: Create an Environment in SAP Build Lobby

What it is: An Environment is the 'home' where your deployed workflows live and run.

Steps:

  1. Go to SAP Build Lobby → Control Tower → Environments
  2. Click Create Environment
  3. Enter an Environment Name and Identifier
  4. Click Create

What to expect: Your environment now appears in the list. You will deploy your approval process here later.

Step 2: Create BTP Destinations

What it is: A Destination is a saved connection that tells BPA how to reach SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 (or any other external system). Without this, BPA cannot call external APIs.

Steps:

  1. Go to your BTP Subaccount → Connectivity → Destinations
  2. Create a new destination for your target system
  3. Add the following mandatory additional parameters to every BPA destination:

    Parameter

    Value

    sap.applicationdevelopment.actions.enabled

    true

    sap.processautomation.enabled

    true

  4. If your destination points to a CAP service, also add:

    Parameter

    Value

    sap.build.usage

    CAP

Beginner Tip: If your destination is scoped to a specific environment, it may not appear in the BPA Actions configuration. To fix this, set the destination to be available for All Environments.

What to expect: Your destination is now ready to be added to BPA.

Step 3: Add BTP Destinations to SAP BPA

Steps:

  1. Go to SAP Build Lobby → Control Tower → Destinations
  2. Click Add
  3. Select the destinations you created in Step 2 from the list

What to expect: BPA can now use these destinations when calling external systems from within your workflow.

Step 4: Create a Service Key in BTP

What it is: A Service Key gives you the credentials (Client ID, Client Secret, Token URL) needed to call BPA APIs from an external system.

Steps:

  1. In your BTP Subaccount, navigate to Services → Instances and Subscriptions
  2. Find your SAP Build Process Automation service instance
  3. Click on it and create a Service Key
  4. Save the generated credentials – you will need them later.

What to expect: You now have the Client ID, Client Secret, and OAuth Token URL needed for API authentication.

Step 5: Create an API Key

What it is: An API Key is a simpler token that external systems (like SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2) use to trigger your BPA workflow.

Steps:

  1. Go to SAP Build Lobby → Control Tower → Environments → (Select your environment) → API Keys
  2. Click Add API Key
  3. Enter a Name and click Next
  4. Select the required scopes and click Next
  5. Review and click Add
  6. Copy the key immediately - you will not be able to see it again after closing this screen

What to expect: You now have an API Key to include in the header of every trigger request from the external system.

Step 6: Create an Action Project

What it is: An Action is a reusable connector that lets you call an external API - for example, to fetch an approver from SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 or to update a record after approval.

Steps:

  1. From SAP Build Lobby, go to Connectors → Actions
  2. Click Create → Choose Build From Scratch
  3. Enter a Project Name and click Create
  4. Add a Custom Action by specifying:
    • The HTTP Operation (GET, POST, PATCH, etc.)
    • A Name for the action
    • The Endpoint URL of the external API
  5. Test your action. Release and Publish.

What to expect: Your Action is now available to be used as a step inside your approval process workflow.

Figure 1: How V2 Connects to SAP BPA 

 

Building the Approval Process

Now that the infrastructure is ready, let's build the actual workflow.

  • Step 1: Create a New Process Automation Project
  • Step 2: Add an API Trigger
  • Step 3: Create Data Types
  • Step 4: Add a Decision (Approval Rules)
  • Step 5: Build the Remaining Process Steps

Let’s see these steps in detail:

Step 1: Create a New Process Automation Project

  1. From SAP Build Lobby, click Create → Select Process Automation
  2. Enter a Project Name and click Create
  3. Inside the project, go to Overview → Artifacts → Create → Process
  4. Enter a Name and Identifier for the process, then click Create

Step 2: Add an API Trigger

What it is: The API Trigger is the entry point of your workflow. When SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 sends a request to this trigger, the approval process starts.

  1. Open your Process
  2. Click Add a Trigger → Select API Trigger
  3. Enter a Name and Identifier, then click Create

Beginner Tip: The trigger URL and example payload are only visible after you deploy the project. You cannot test it before deployment.

Step 3: Create Data Types

What it is: Data Types define the structure of the information flowing through your workflow - like defining the columns of a spreadsheet before filling it in.

You need two Data Types:

  1. API Trigger Input - the fields coming in from SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 (e.g., object ID, initiator, condition values, default approver)
  2. Decision Table Output - the fields your approval rules will return

Recommended Decision Table Output structure:

Field

Type

What It Means

IsApprovalRequired

Boolean (True/False)

Is approval needed for this record?

level1

Text

Approver ID for the first approval level

level2

Text

Approver ID for the second approval level (if needed)

You can add more levels (e.g., level3) as your business rules require.

Step 4: Add a Decision (Approval Rules)

What it is: The Decision artifact is where you define your approval rules using a Decision Table - essentially a structured 'if-then' table.

Example logic:

  • IF the deal value is above a threshold → IsApprovalRequired = true, level1 = Manager ID
  • IF the deal value is below the threshold → IsApprovalRequired = false
  1. Inside your project, go to Artifacts → Create → Decision
  2. Define your input fields (from the API Trigger Input Data Type)
  3. Define your output fields (from the Decision Table Output Data Type)
  4. Fill in the rules row by row in the Decision Table

Step 5: Build the Remaining Process Steps

After the Decision step, add the following steps based on your requirements:

  1. Condition check - If IsApprovalRequired = true, proceed to approval; otherwise, auto-approve
  2. Action step (Before Approval) - Update the BO status to 'Pending Approval' in SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2
  3. Approval Task - Assign to the approver identified in level1 (and level2 if multi-level)
  4. Action step (After Approval) - Update the BO status to 'Approved' or 'Rejected' in SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2

Common Scenarios

Scenario A: Simple Static Approver

  • When to use this: The approver is already stored as a field in the Business Object (e.g., a 'Manager' field on a Sales Quote)
  • How it works: Pass the approver's ID directly in the API trigger payload - no additional lookup needed
  • Best for: Simple, predictable approval chains where the approver doesn't change dynamically

Scenario B: Approver from Org Hierarchy in SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2

  • When to use this: The approver needs to be determined dynamically based on the organizational hierarchy at the time of the approval request
  • How it works: Add a BPA Action step that calls the SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 Org Hierarchy API to retrieve the correct approver at runtime
  • Best for: Organizations where reporting lines determine who approves

Scenario C: Programmatic Approve/Reject via API (No UI Needed)

  • When to use this: You want an external system to approve or reject tasks automatically, without a human clicking a button in My Inbox
  • How it works - 3 steps:
    1. Trigger the workflow → The API response returns the Workflow Instance ID
    2. Query the task list using the Instance ID → This returns the Task ID of the pending approval task
    3. PATCH the task using the Task ID → Send the approval decision (Approve/Reject)
  • Best for: Automated or system-driven approval scenarios

Scenario D : Multi-Level Approval

  • When to use this: Some records require approval from more than one person (e.g., Manager → Director)
  • How it works: The Decision Table returns both level1 and level2 approver IDs. The process flow includes sequential approval tasks - first for level1, then for level2
  • Best for: High-value transactions or regulated processes requiring multiple sign-offs

How to Trigger the Workflow from an External System

For standard business objects, SAP Build Process Automation (BPA) workflows can be initiated through Autoflow configured in SAP Sales and Service Cloud Version 2. For custom business objects developed on SAP BTP using CAP, BPA workflows are typically invoked from the CAP application logic in response to business events such as create or update operations.

Once your project is released and deployed, follow these steps to find the trigger URL and test the end-to-end flow:

Find the Trigger URL:

  1. Go to SAP Build Lobby → Control Tower → Environments → (Select your environment) → Triggers
  2. Click the ⋮ (three dots) next to your trigger → Select View
  3. Copy the Trigger URL and the Example Payload

Test using Bruno (API Client):

Setting

Value

Method

POST

URL

Trigger URL from above

Header: irpa-api-key

Your API Key

Auth Type

OAuth 2.0 – Client Credentials

Access Token URL

<Service Key URL>/oauth/token

Client ID

From your Service Key

Client Secret

From your Service Key

Add Credentials To

Request Body

Add Token To

Headers (Bearer)

Get the Access Token first, then use it to send the POST request with the Example Payload.

Sample Payload:

{
    "definitionId": "<region>.<btp-subaccount-id>.<project-name>.<process-name>.approvalProcess",
    "context": {
        "requestinfo": {
            "ObjectID": "",
            "RequestDisplayID": "",
            "DiscountPercent": 0,
            "Amount": 0,
            "CurrencyCode": "",
            "Initiator": "",
            "Partner": "",
            "Description": ""
        }
    }
}

 Figure 2: Sample Payload

The exact structure of the trigger payload depends on the API Trigger Input Data Type you defined in Step 3 (Create Data Types). There is no single fixed payload - it will reflect the fields you configured, such as object ID, initiator, condition values, and default approver.

Beginner Tip: If you later add or change fields in your API Trigger Input Data Type and redeploy, revisit this screen to get the updated example payload.

Troubleshooting Common Issues

Problem

Solution

Destination not visible in BPA Actions

Change the destination scope from a specific environment to All Environments in BTP

API Trigger URL not visible

The trigger only appears after the project is released and deployed to an environment

API Key lost or forgotten

API Keys cannot be retrieved after creation - create a new one via Control Tower → Environments → API Keys

Approval status not updating in SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2

Ensure you have Action steps configured both before and after the approval task to sync the status

Email notifications not working

SMTP configuration and Azure AD setup are required prerequisites - confirm these are in place before testing

Dynamic task links not working in approval emails

This is a known limitation - only static links are currently supported in BPA email notifications. See: SAP Community Reference

Complex approver logic causing process errors

Move complex approver determination logic outside of BPA (e.g., into the source system or a dedicated service) and pass the result into BPA via the trigger payload

Key Design Considerations

Before implementing your approval process, be aware of the following design considerations:

  • For standard BOs in V2 that support approvals natively, the approve/reject action and notifications are handled within the V2 application itself.
  • For custom BOs or BPA-driven approval processes, approvers access tasks via SAP Task Center or BPA My Inbox - not from within V2.
  • Email notifications require SMTP + Azure AD (or Google Workspace) configuration - this is not automatic.
  • Dynamic task links in emails are not supported - only static links can be included.
  • BPA does not come pre-configured - all workflow logic must be built by the customer or implementation partner.
  • A BPA license is required to use external approval processes with SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2.

Ready to get started? Pick your simplest approval scenario, follow the prerequisite steps in order, deploy to a test environment, and validate the full end-to-end flow. Once that works, you will have the confidence and the blueprint to tackle more complex scenarios with ease.

entry.title: V1-V2 Transition: A Consultant's Playbook — Part 2: Getting Into the Weeds (The Lite Assessment)
entry.content:
V1-V2 Transition: A Consultant's Playbook
-  Part 2: Getting Into the Weeds (The Lite Assessment)

This is Part 2 of a multi-part series on planning and executing a phased SAP Sales & Service Cloud V1-to-V2 transition. If you haven't read it yet, Part 1 covers the Pre-Assessment  the feature parity check that decides whether a customer can move to V2 at all, and what's still blocking them if not. Part 3 will cover execution.

Same disclaimer as last time: this isn't an official SAP best-practice guide. It's a look into how I personally run a Lite Assessment the decisions I make, the workshops I run, and the reasoning behind them based on my own experience as a consultant, not a prescribed methodology.

A note on accuracy: everything here screenshots, tool details, deliverable names, feature availability  reflects a snapshot in time. SAP's tools, product roadmap, and feature set keep evolving, so details may have changed by the time you're reading this. I take no liability for the accuracy of the images and information shown; always verify current specifics with SAP or your own project team.

Quick recap, in case you're joining here: the Pre-Assessment answers "can we go, and if not, what's blocking us?" It's deliberately lightweight a couple of weeks, mostly document-driven, no deep code analysis involved and it's a free SAP service. The Lite Assessment is a different animal entirely, and it's worth flagging that it's a paid SAP service (as is the Deep Assessment) a customer is booking real, dedicated effort at this point, not just a readiness check. Content-wise, it's where I stop asking "can we go" and start asking "what will it actually take?"

Running a Lite Assessment: My Way Through It

The Pre-Assessment is something I largely run from my desk documents, an Excel export, maybe a call or two. The Lite Assessment is the opposite: it's hands-on, workshop-driven, and it only works if I actually sit down with the people who use the system every day. Below is how I actually run one, start to finish, and what the customer walks away with at the end.

On bigger engagements, this isn't a one-person show. A typical Lite or Deep Assessment team splits into a few roles: a functional consultant who owns the business process review and leads the process deep dive workshops, a technical/extensibility consultant who runs the AssessMate analysis on custom code and objects and walks the customer through tools like TransforMate and CBOM, and an integration consultant who covers standard and custom integrations. Depending on the engagement, I've played more than one of those roles myself — but I'll walk through the path end to end here, since that's the part that matters for understanding the assessment, regardless of how many people are actually in the room.

Step 1: Scoping the Engagement

The Lite Assessment is a fee-based service, and I never quote a duration off the top of my head — it depends heavily on the outcome of the Pre-Assessment questionnaire. One detail that matters more than people expect: whether the customer has already completed a Pre-Assessment (itself about two person-days of effort), and just as important, whether that Pre-Assessment is still recent. Anything older than three months, and I treat the picture as stale rather than build a Lite Assessment timeline on top of it.

I also make a point of being upfront about what's not included by default. Approvals, forms, mass data runs, custom code lists, and UI Designer extensions aren't part of a standard Lite Assessment — and a small number of other objects a customer might be using are excluded too, documented separately in a dedicated scope document. All of that can be added to the engagement, but it's a paid extension of scope, not something bundled in from the start. I'd rather have that conversation in week one than have a customer discover in the final presentation that something they use daily was never actually assessed.

Step 2: Kick-Off

Before any workshop gets scheduled, I go back through the Pre-Assessment material — specifically the system complexity signal from the Discovery Questionnaire — to sharpen my first duration estimate into something concrete. That estimate shapes everything that follows: how many workshops I plan, how they're spread across weeks, and who needs to be in the room.

With that estimate in hand, I either set up a short kick-off meeting or simply send an email covering the essentials: the next steps, what the customer needs to prepare ahead of the Business Process Deep Dive sessions, a first draft agenda, and proposed dates. I'd rather over-communicate at this stage than have a workshop stall because nobody knew what to bring.

Scope for these workshops comes straight out of the Pre-Assessment documentation the process areas the customer flagged as in use. If I need a scope check without digging through paperwork, there's a faster route too: opening the Readiness Check report directly in the customer's C4C system and looking at which objects actually carry data records. An object with records behind it is genuinely in use; one without is a fast way to cut scope down before I've scheduled a single workshop.

Only once the customer and I are aligned on next steps, prerequisites
and dates does the first Deep Dive workshop actually start.

Step 3: Running AssessMate on the Custom Code

Somewhere around the same time the workshops kick off, I also run the customer's PDI ABSL scripts and custom business objects through AssessMate. It is an AI-powered PDI Migration Advisor build by SAP. Its purpose-built for V1-to-V2 Move engagements. It analyzes what's actually deployed and generates high-level effort estimates for migrating it into the clean-core, BTP-based CAP extension model that V2 expects. That reframing matters: migrating custom extensions isn't a lift-and-shift, it's a redesign, and AssessMate is what gives me a data-driven read on how big that redesign effort actually is.

Concretely, AssessMate gives me:

  • A business and technical summary of every ABSL script
  • A code complexity classification, based on an LLM analysis of factors like the number of database queries, BO instances created, web service calls, standard and custom actions invoked, and the complexity of V1-to-V2 field mapping
  • A view of custom business objects, including their structure (simple vs. hierarchical), field counts, and whether they carry their own business logic
  • A recommended migration approach for example, whether an External Hook or an Autoflow pattern fits best on BTP/SSC V2
  • Data model mapping between V1 and V2 objects, which surfaces redesign needs early
  • High-level effort estimates for the migration work itself

There's an important boundary here, though: AssessMate only estimates effort for the customer's specific, custom-code extensions PDI ABSL scripts and custom business objects. It has nothing to say about standard configuration. Estimating how much effort standard configuration work will take still comes down to an experienced SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2 consultant, judging based on their own hands-on experience. AssessMate narrows the guesswork on the custom side; the standard-configuration side still runs on consultant judgment and that split matters a lot once I get to the
T-shirt size estimate at the end of this post.

What I value most about AssessMate isn't just the speed though compressing what used to be weeks of manual ABSL review into days is a real difference it's the consistency it brings to the custom-code estimate specifically. The effort estimate for a given script or object no longer depends on which consultant happened to review it.

Step 4: The Business Process Deep Dive Workshops

This is the part of the Lite Assessment I'd genuinely fight to keep in scope, even under time pressure.

A Readiness Check report or an AssessMate complexity rating can tell you that a customization exists and roughly how complex it is to migrate. Neither can tell you why it exists. And without the "why," you're migrating code not a business process.

Take Lead Management, a process I've run this workshop for many times. I sit down with the customer's process owner and let them walk me through how they actually run leads in their organization and not how the SAP standard process assumes they do. Step by step, I'm listening for where their process deviates from standard, and asking, at each deviation: why did you build a customer-specific extension here? Often the answer reveals a genuine business requirement the standard process doesn't cover. Just as often, it reveals a workaround for a limitation that no longer exists in V2, or a habit that formed years ago for reasons nobody quite remembers anymore.

I run this same style of workshop for every business process object in the customer's scope.
Account & Contact Management, Activity Management, Opportunity Management, Ticket Management, whatever the Pre-Assessment flagged as in use.

That distinction changes everything about my recommendation. If I understand why a customization was made, I can tell the customer whether V2 already solves that need natively, whether a different standard feature achieves the same outcome, or whether a genuine extension is still required and if so, what shape it should take. Without that context, I'd be forced to recommend rebuilding every customization as-is, which almost always means carrying forward complexity that V2 was specifically designed to eliminate.

Example Business process deep dive workshop (Example: Plan Visit process)

 

Step 5: Integrations and the Target Architecture

Integrations and mashups get their own workshop, run the same way — walking through what's connected today and why. Once I know which systems are connected, which recommendations came out of that review, and which supporting systems are involved, I put together a high-level target application architecture diagram a single picture the customer can hold onto that shows how everything is meant to connect once the transition is done.

Example: Target application architecture diagram

 

Step 6: Turning Workshops Into Recommendations

After every business process conversation, I note the specifics the deviation, the reasoning behind it, and anything that stood out — directly in my Lite Assessment report. Once all the process workshops are done, I sit down with those notes and turn them into actual recommendations, structured the same way for every finding: the business process, the key pain point or finding, my recommendation, the recommended target solution, and because this genuinely varies its availability: already available in standard V2, planned on the roadmap, requiring a custom build, or a new capability the customer hasn't used before.

The recommendation itself is where I try to go a step further than just checking a box for "does V2 cover this." Sometimes the honest answer is yes, V2 covers it natively, done. But sometimes there's more value in flagging a new V2 AI feature that doesn't just replicate the old process but genuinely improves it a generative summary, a predictive score, something the customer never had in V1 at all. And sometimes the right recommendation isn't "stay inside Sales & Service Cloud" at all it might be pulling in SAP BTP Integration Suite for a specific integration pattern, or using SAP Analytics Cloud, embedded directly in V2, to replace a custom reporting object rather than trying to rebuild it like-for-like.

Example: Business process findings & recommendations table

 

The Deliverables I Actually Hand Over

By the time all the workshops are done and AssessMate has processed the custom code,
what the customer gets isn't just "a workshop and a slide deck"  it's a defined set of deliverables:

  • An executive summary of the assessment findings, alongside a feature parity result list
  • The business process review across Sales and Service, with the recommendations from Step 6
  • The standard integration and mashup review, resulting in the target architecture diagram from Step 5 and a set of integration recommendations
  • The custom code review a human-readable description of what the customer's ABSL scripts actually do,
    recommendations, and the AssessMate-driven effort estimate from Step 3
  • An overview of standard reporting capabilities in V2
  • A data and configuration migration plan and timeline
  • A transformation roadmap
  • Next steps

And, tying all of the above together, a T-shirt size effort estimate — which is worth its own explanation, because it's not a single number I pull from one tool.

Example: Executive summary 

 

How the T-Shirt Size Effort Estimate Actually Comes Together

This is the question customers ask most directly at the end of a Lite Assessment: "so, how much work is this?" The honest answer is that the T-shirt size is a combination of two separate estimates, covering two separate scopes and keeping them separate is exactly what makes the number defensible.

The first scope is everything that needs to be migrated: the customer's custom-code extensions PDI ABSL scripts and custom business objects that came out of Step 3. That's AssessMate's estimate, object by object and script by script, based on actual code complexity rather than guesswork.

The second scope is everything that needs to be configured: the standard business objects and process areas the customer actually uses, identified back in the Pre-Assessment and confirmed in the Step 4 workshops. AssessMate has nothing to say about this side configuring standard V2 to match a customer's process areas is estimated the way it's always been estimated, by an experienced SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2 consultant drawing on hands-on delivery experience with comparable scopes.

The T-shirt size I hand the customer is the combination of those two: the AssessMate-driven effort for the migrate-scope, plus my own experience-based effort for the configure-scope. I'm always upfront that it's informative rather than final — it's built to give the customer and whoever's approving the next phase a realistic order of magnitude, not a fixed-price commitment. Verifying it in detail is exactly what a Deep Assessment is for, which is why I never present a T-shirt size without that caveat attached.

By the end of the Lite Assessment, I have something the Pre-Assessment alone could never produce: a process-level understanding of the customer's business, paired with a much sharper, evidence-based recommendation for how each deviation should be handled in V2 and a T-shirt size estimate the customer can actually plan around, because they know exactly what it's made of.

Where This Leaves Us

At this point in the journey, I've moved from "here's roughly what exists and roughly how hard it is" to "here's what the customer's business actually needs, and here's the concrete path to get it into V2." That's the foundation everything else in the transition gets built on.

In Part 3, I'll walk through how I take this preparation work — Pre-Assessment and Lite Assessment together — and turn it into an actual transition: in my case, that means going live with Service Cloud first and Sales Cloud second, and I'll document how the migration plan and everything gathered in the previous assessments actually gets used once execution starts — the concrete steps I take to carry out the V1-to-V2 transition itself.

Stay tune for Part 3

If you missed it, Part 1 covers the Pre-Assessment in full.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This post reflects my personal approach and experience as a consultant, and does not represent official SAP guidance. It is a snapshot in time — screenshots, tool details, and roadmap information may no longer be current, and I accept no liability for their accuracy. Feedback and differing perspectives are very welcome in the comments.
