V1-V2 Transition: A Consultant's Playbook
— Part 2: Getting Into the Weeds (The Lite Assessment)

This is Part 2 of a multi-part series on planning and executing a phased SAP Sales & Service Cloud V1-to-V2 transition. If you haven't read it yet, Part 1 "V1-V2 Transition: A Consultant's Playbook - Part 1: Know Before You Go (The Pre-Assessment)" covers the Pre-Assessment and the feature parity check that decides whether a customer can move to V2 at all, and what's still blocking them if not. Part 3 will cover execution.

 

Same disclaimer as last time: this isn't an official SAP best-practice guide. It's a look into how I personally run a Lite Assessment and the decisions I make, the workshops I run, and the reasoning behind them based on my own experience as a consultant, not a prescribed methodology.

A note on accuracy: everything here  screenshots, tool details, deliverable and tool names, feature availability reflects a snapshot in time. SAP's tools, product roadmap, and feature set keep evolving, so details may have changed by the time you're reading this. I take no liability for the accuracy of the images and information shown; always verify current specifics with SAP or your own project team.

Quick recap, in case you're joining here: the Pre-Assessment answers "can we go, and if not, what's blocking us?" It's deliberately lightweight — a couple of days, mostly document-driven, no deep code analysis involved and it's a free SAP service. The Lite Assessment is a different animal entirely, and it's worth flagging that it's a paid SAP service (as is the Deep Assessment)  a customer is booking real, dedicated effort at this point, not just a readiness check. Content-wise, it's where I stop asking "can we go" and start asking "what will it actually take?"

Running a Lite Assessment: My Way Through It

The Pre-Assessment is something I largely run from my desk documents, an Excel export, maybe a call or two. The Lite Assessment is the opposite: it's hands-on, workshop-driven, and it only works if I actually sit down with the people who use the system every day. Below is how I actually run one, start to finish, and what the customer walks away with at the end.

On bigger engagements, this isn't a one-person show. A typical Lite or Deep Assessment team splits into a few roles: a functional consultant who owns the business process review and leads the process deep dive workshops, a technical/extensibility consultant who runs an SAP-internal AI code-analysis tool over the custom code and objects and walks the customer through tools like TransforMate and CBOM, and an integration consultant who covers standard and custom integrations. Depending on the engagement, I've played more than one of those roles myself but I'll walk through the path end to end here, since that's the part that matters for understanding the assessment, regardless of how many people are actually in the room.

Step 1: Scoping the Engagement

The Lite Assessment is a fee-based service, and I never quote a duration off the top of my head, it depends heavily on the outcome of the Pre-Assessment questionnaire. One detail that matters more than people expect: whether the customer has already completed a Pre-Assessment (itself about two person-days of effort), and just as important, whether that Pre-Assessment is still recent. Anything older than three months, and I treat the picture as stale rather than build a Lite Assessment timeline on top of it.

I also make a point of being upfront about what's not included by default. Approvals, forms, mass data runs, custom code lists, and UI Designer extensions aren't part of a standard Lite Assessment and a small number of other objects a customer might be using are excluded too, documented separately in a dedicated scope document. All of that can be added to the engagement, but it's a paid extension of scope, not something bundled in from the start. I'd rather have that conversation in week one than have a customer discover in the final presentation that something they use daily was never actually assessed.

Step 2: Kick-Off

Before any workshop gets scheduled, I go back through the Pre-Assessment material — specifically the system complexity signal from the Discovery Questionnaire — to sharpen my first duration estimate into something concrete. That estimate shapes everything that follows: how many workshops I plan, how they're spread across weeks, and who needs to be in the room.

With that estimate in hand, I either set up a short kick-off meeting or simply send an email covering the essentials: the next steps, what the customer needs to prepare ahead of the Business Process Deep Dive sessions, a first draft agenda, and proposed dates. I'd rather over-communicate at this stage than have a workshop stall because nobody knew what to bring.

Scope for these workshops comes straight out of the Pre-Assessment documentation the process areas the customer flagged as in use. If I need a scope check without digging through paperwork, there's a faster route too: opening the Readiness Check report directly in the customer's C4C system and looking at which objects actually carry data records. An object with records behind it is genuinely in use; one without is a fast way to cut scope down before I've scheduled a single workshop.

Only once the customer and I are aligned on next steps, prerequisites, and dates does the first Deep Dive workshop actually start.

Step 3: Running the Custom Code Through SAP's Internal AI Tool

Somewhere around the same time the workshops kick off, I also run the customer's PDI ABSL scripts and custom business objects through an SAP-internal AI code-analysis tool built specifically for V1-to-V2 Move engagements. It's not something a customer or partner can access directly it's available to SAP consultants only. It analyzes what's actually deployed and generates high-level effort estimates for migrating it into the clean-core, BTP-based CAP extension model that V2 expects. That reframing matters: migrating custom extensions isn't a lift-and-shift, it's a redesign, and this tool is what gives me a data-driven read on how big that redesign effort actually is.

Concretely, it gives me:

  • A business and technical summary of every ABSL script
  • A code complexity classification, based on an LLM analysis of factors like the number of database queries, BO instances created, web service calls, standard and custom actions invoked, and the complexity of V1-to-V2 field mapping
  • A view of custom business objects, including their structure (simple vs. hierarchical), field counts, and whether they carry their own business logic
  • A recommended migration approach — for example, whether an External Hook or an Autoflow pattern fits best on BTP/SSC V2
  • Data model mapping between V1 and V2 objects, which surfaces redesign needs early
  • High-level effort estimates for the migration work itself

There's an important boundary here, though: this tool only estimates effort for the customer's specific, custom-code extensions PDI ABSL scripts and custom business objects. It has nothing to say about standard configuration. Estimating how much effort standard configuration work will take still comes down to an experienced SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2 consultant, judging based on their own hands-on experience. The AI tool narrows the guesswork on the custom side; the standard-configuration side still runs on consultant judgment and that split matters a lot once I get to the T-shirt size estimate at the end of this post.

What I value most about it isn't just the speed though compressing what used to be weeks of manual ABSL review into days is a real difference it's the consistency it brings to the custom-code estimate specifically. The effort estimate for a given script or object no longer depends on which consultant happened to review it.

Step 4: The Business Process Deep Dive Workshops

This is the part of the Lite Assessment I'd genuinely fight to keep in scope, even under time pressure.

A Readiness Check report or an AI-generated complexity rating from that internal tool can tell you that a customization exists and roughly how complex it is to migrate. Neither can tell you why it exists. And without the "why," you're migrating code not a business process.

Take Lead Management, a process I've run this workshop for many times. I sit down with the customer's process owner and let them walk me through how they actually run leads in their organization — not how the SAP standard process assumes they do. Step by step, I'm listening for where their process deviates from standard, and asking, at each deviation: why did you build a customer-specific extension here? Often the answer reveals a genuine business requirement the standard process doesn't cover. Just as often, it reveals a workaround for a limitation that no longer exists in V2, or a habit that formed years ago for reasons nobody quite remembers anymore.

I run this same style of workshop for every business process object in the customer's scope Account & Contact Management, Activity Management, Opportunity Management, Ticket Management, whatever the Pre-Assessment flagged as in use.

That distinction changes everything about my recommendation. If I understand why a customization was made, I can tell the customer whether V2 already solves that need natively, whether a different standard feature achieves the same outcome, or whether a genuine extension is still required and if so, what shape it should take. Without that context, I'd be forced to recommend rebuilding every customization as-is, which almost always means carrying forward complexity that V2 was specifically designed to eliminate.

Business process deep dive workshop – Account & Contact Management (Mural example)

 

Step 5: Integrations and the Target Architecture

Integrations and mashups get their own workshop, run the same way  walking through what's connected today and why. Once I know which systems are connected, which recommendations came out of that review, and which supporting systems are involved, I put together a high-level target application architecture diagram a single picture the customer can hold onto that shows how everything is meant to connect once the transition is done.

Application architecture diagram (example)

 

Step 6: Turning Workshops Into Recommendations

After every business process conversation, I note the specifics and the deviation, the reasoning behind it, and anything that stood out directly in my Lite Assessment report. Once all the process workshops are done, I sit down with those notes and turn them into actual recommendations, structured the same way for every finding: the business process, the key pain point or finding, my recommendation, the recommended target solution, and because this genuinely varies its availability: already available in standard V2, planned on the roadmap, requiring a custom build, or a new capability the customer hasn't used before.

The recommendation itself is where I try to go a step further than just checking a box for "does V2 cover this." Sometimes the honest answer is yes, V2 covers it natively, done. But sometimes there's more value in flagging a new V2 AI feature that doesn't just replicate the old process but genuinely improves it, a generative summary, a predictive score, something the customer never had in V1 at all. And sometimes the right recommendation isn't "stay inside Sales & Service Cloud" at all it might be pulling in SAP BTP Integration Suite for a specific integration pattern, or using SAP Analytics Cloud, embedded directly in V2, to replace a custom reporting object rather than trying to rebuild it like-for-like.

(Example) Business process findings & recommendations table

 

The Deliverables I Actually Hand Over

By the time all the workshops are done and the internal AI tool has processed the custom code, what the customer gets isn't just "a workshop and a slide deck" — it's a defined set of deliverables:

  • An executive summary of the assessment findings, alongside a feature parity result list
  • The business process review across Sales and Service, with the recommendations from Step 6
  • The integration and mashup review, resulting in the target architecture diagram from Step 5 and a set of integration recommendations
  • The custom code review a human-readable description of what the customer's ABSL scripts actually do, recommendations, and the AI-tool-driven effort estimate from Step 3
  • An overview of standard reporting capabilities in V2
  • A data and configuration migration plan and timeline
  • A transformation roadmap
  • Next steps

And, tying all of the above together, a T-shirt size effort estimate — which is worth its own explanation, because it's not a single number I pull from one tool.

(EXAMPLE) Executive summary



How the T-Shirt Size Effort Estimate Actually Comes Together

This is the question customers ask most directly at the end of a Lite Assessment: "so, how much work is this?" The honest answer is that the T-shirt size is a combination of two separate estimates, covering two separate scopes and keeping them separate is exactly what makes the number defensible.

The first scope is everything that needs to be migrated: the customer's custom-code extensions PDI ABSL scripts and custom business objects that came out of Step 3. That's the internal AI tool's estimate, object by object and script by script, based on actual code complexity rather than guesswork.

The second scope is everything that needs to be configured: the standard business objects and process areas the customer actually uses, identified back in the Pre-Assessment and confirmed in the Step 4 workshops. That internal tool has nothing to say about this side configuring standard V2 to match a customer's process areas is estimated the way it's always been estimated, by an experienced SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2 consultant drawing on hands-on delivery experience with comparable scopes.

The T-shirt size I hand the customer is the combination of those two: the AI-tool-driven effort for the migrate-scope, plus my own experience-based effort for the configure-scope. I'm always upfront that it's informative rather than final it's built to give the customer and whoever's approving the next phase a realistic order of magnitude, not a fixed-price commitment. Verifying it in detail is exactly what a Deep Assessment is for, which is why I never present a T-shirt size without that caveat attached.

By the end of the Lite Assessment, I have something the Pre-Assessment alone could never produce: a process-level understanding of the customer's business, paired with a much sharper, evidence-based recommendation for how each deviation should be handled in V2 and a T-shirt size estimate the customer can actually plan around, because they know exactly what it's made of.

Where This Leaves Us

At this point in the journey, I've moved from "here's roughly what exists and roughly how hard it is" to "here's what the customer's business actually needs, and here's the concrete path to get it into V2." That's the foundation everything else in the transition gets built on.

In Part 3, I’ll walk through how I take this preparation work, Pre-Assessment and Lite Assessment together, and turn it into an actual phased transition. I’ll follow the Phased Go-Live approach exactly as described in the SAP Help documentation for the Data Transfer Tool: in my case, that means phasing by organizational unit. All data is transferred with one initial load and kept in sync with delta loads, while ACL restrictions in V1 and V2 define which org unit works in which system during each phase.

This post reflects my personal approach and experience as a consultant, and does not represent official SAP guidance. Feedback and differing perspectives are very welcome in the comments.

entry.title: From SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 APIs to AI: Building an MCP Server with CAP Node.js
entry.content:
Overview

Model Context Protocol (MCP) provides a standardized way for AI applications to interact with external tools and business data.

In this tutorial, we will build a CAP Node.js application that consumes the SAP Sales Cloud V2 Case API, exposes selected case operations through a CAP service, and makes those operations available through an MCP endpoint.

The resulting solution allows an MCP-compatible AI client to interact with SAP Sales Cloud V2 cases using tools such as:

  • List cases
  • Search and filter cases
  • Retrieve a case by ID
  • Create a new case
  • Update an existing case

Prerequisites

Before starting, make sure you have:

  • SAP BTP account with Cloud Foundry environment
  • SAP Sales Cloud V2 tenant
  • Access to the Sales Cloud V2 Case API
  • Node.js installed
  • SAP CAP development environment
  • Cloud Foundry CLI
  • VS Code
  • Appropriate authentication credentials or a BTP destination for the Sales Cloud V2 system

Step 1 — Create a CAP Node.js Project

Create a new CAP project:

cds init cx-mcp --nodejs
cd cx-mcp
code .

Install the project dependencies:

npm install

The basic project structure will look similar to:

cx-mcp/
├── app/
├── db/
├── srv/
├── package.json
└── README.md

Step 2 — Add the SAP Sales Cloud V2 Case API

The next step is to make the Sales Cloud V2 Case API available as a remote service in CAP.

For example, the external service can be maintained under:

srv/external/SalesSvcCloudV2_case.cds

The external service represents the Case API exposed by SAP Sales Cloud V2.

Once the external API is available, we can consume it from our CAP service.

The important concept here is that CAP acts as the integration layer between the MCP interface and SAP Sales Cloud V2.

MCP Client
    |
    v
CAP Service
    |
    v
External Case Service
    |
    v
SAP Sales Cloud V2

Step 3 — Define the CX Case Service

Create:

srv/caseservices.cds

The service defines the operations that we want to expose to both OData and MCP clients.

using { Service as c4c } from './external/SalesSvcCloudV2_case';

@title: 'Case Service'
@description: 'Manages service and support cases from SAP Sales Cloud V2 (C4C).'
service caseservices {

    type CaseItem {
        id              : UUID;
        displayId       : String(35);
        subject         : String;
        priority        : String;
        status          : String;
        lifeCycleStatus : String;
        caseType        : String;
        createdOn       : Timestamp;
        updatedOn       : Timestamp;
    }

    type CaseInput {
        subject               : String;
        priority              : String;
        status                : String;
        caseType              : String;
        communicationLanguage : String;
    }

    @title: 'List Cases'
    @description: 'Query cases from SAP Sales Cloud V2. Supports $top, $skip, $filter, $search.'
    function listCases(
        _top    : Integer,
        _skip   : Integer,
        _filter : String,
        _search : String
    ) returns many CaseItem;

    @title: 'Get Case by ID'
    @description: 'Retrieve a single case by its UUID.'
    function getCaseById(id: UUID) returns CaseItem;

    @title: 'Create Case'
    @description: 'Create a new service case in SAP Sales Cloud V2.'
    action createCase(body: CaseInput) returns CaseItem;

    @title: 'Patch Case'
    @description: 'Partially update an existing case by its UUID.'
    action patchCase(
        id   : UUID,
        body : CaseInput
    ) returns CaseItem;
}

annotate caseservices with @protocol: [
    'odata-v4',
    'mcp'
];

The important part is the following annotation:

annotate caseservices with @protocol: [
    'odata-v4',
    'mcp'
];

This allows the same CAP service to be exposed through both OData V4 and MCP.

Step 4 — Configure the Remote Service

The CAP application needs to know how to connect to SAP Sales Cloud V2.

The configuration can be maintained in package.json.

For a local/hybrid setup, you can configure the remote service credentials under a hybrid profile.

For example:

{
  "cds": {
    "requires": {
      "SalesSvcCloudV2_case": {
        "kind": "odata-v4",
        "model": "srv/external/SalesSvcCloudV2_case",
        "[hybrid]": {
          "credentials": {
            "url": "<SALES-CLOUD-V2-URL>",
            "authentication": "BasicAuthentication",
            "username": "<USERNAME>",
            "password": "<PASSWORD>"
          }
        },
        "[production]": {
          "credentials": {
            "destination": "CX-SALES-CLOUD-V2",
            "path": "<CASE-API-PATH>"
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

For a production deployment, it is recommended to use a BTP destination rather than hard-coding credentials in the application.

Step 5 — Implement the Case Service Handler

Create:

srv/caseservices.js

The service handler connects to the remote SAP Sales Cloud V2 service and implements the business operations.

const cds = require("@sap/cds");

class CaseService extends cds.ApplicationService {

    async init() {

        const c4c = await cds.connect.to("SalesSvcCloudV2_case");

        this.on("listCases", async (req) => {

            const {
                _top,
                _skip,
                _filter,
                _search
            } = req.data;

            // Build the query against the remote Case API.
            // The exact entity/path should match the imported
            // SAP Sales Cloud V2 Case service definition.

            let query = SELECT.from(c4c.entities.Case);

            if (_filter) {
                query.where(_filter);
            }

            if (_top) {
                query.limit(_top, _skip || 0);
            }

            return c4c.run(query);
        });
     
        return super.init();
    }
}

module.exports = {
    caseservices: CaseService
};

///    Similarly write for [getCaseById,createCase,patchCase]  ///////////////////

Note: The exact remote entity name, key field and service path depend on the imported SalesSvcCloudV2_case.cds definition. Adjust c4c.entities.Case and the field mappings according to the generated external service metadata.

Step 6 — Add MCP Support

Install the CAP MCP package:

npm add @cap-js/mcp

You can also add XSUAA and MTA support if you plan to deploy the application to SAP BTP:

cds add xsuaa
cds add mta

The MCP configuration can be enabled in package.json:

{
  "cds": {
    "mcp": {
      "per_action_tool": true
    }
  }
}

With MCP enabled, CAP can expose the service operations as MCP tools.

The resulting endpoint will be:

/mcp/caseservices

Step 7 — Start the Application Locally

Run the application using the hybrid profile:

cds watch

The CAP server should start on:

http://localhost:4004

Your OData service will be available at:

http://localhost:4004/odata/v4/caseservices

The metadata endpoint is:

http://localhost:4004/odata/v4/caseservices/$metadata

The MCP endpoint is:

http://localhost:4004/mcp/caseservices
 

 

 

Step 8 — Explore the OData Service

Open:

http://localhost:4004/odata/v4/caseservices/$metadata

You can use the OData endpoints to test the service.

List Cases

GET /odata/v4/caseservices/listCases

Get Case

GET /odata/v4/caseservices/getCaseById(id=<UUID>)

Create Case

POST /odata/v4/caseservices/createCase

Example payload:

{
    "subject": "Customer unable to access service",
    "priority": "HIGH",
    "status": "OPEN",
    "caseType": "SERVICE_REQUEST",
    "communicationLanguage": "EN"
}

Patch Case

POST /odata/v4/caseservices/patchCase

Example:

{
    "id": "<CASE-UUID>",
    "body": {
        "priority": "HIGH",
        "status": "IN_PROCESS"
    }
}

 

Step 9 — Test with an MCP Client

Once the MCP endpoint is running, it can be connected to an MCP-compatible client.

The client discovers the available tools through:

tools/list

For example, the client may discover:

listCases
getCaseById
createCase
patchCase

The AI application can then translate a natural-language request such as:

"Show me the latest 10 high-priority service cases."

into an MCP tool invocation.

Conceptually:

User
 |
 | "Show me the latest 5 open cases"
 v
AI Application
 |
 | listCases
 | _top = 10
 | _filter = status eq 'open'
 v
MCP
 |
 v
CAP
 |
 v
SAP Sales Cloud V2

 

Step 10— Deploy to SAP BTP Cloud Foundry

Add in desktop for testing as local agent

 

 

Conclusion

In this tutorial, we created a CAP Node.js service that acts as an integration layer between SAP Sales Cloud V2 and MCP-compatible AI applications.

The solution exposes the CX Case capabilities through:

OData V4
    |
    +-- /odata/v4/caseservices
    |
    +-- listCases
    +-- getCaseById
    +-- createCase
    +-- patchCase

MCP
    |
    +-- /mcp/caseservices
    |
    +-- listCases
    +-- getCaseById
    +-- createCase
    +-- patchCase

This approach provides a controlled way to expose SAP CX business capabilities to AI applications while keeping the underlying SAP Sales Cloud V2 integration logic inside the CAP service.

The same pattern can also be extended to other SAP CX business objects and operations, allowing organizations to gradually expose their SAP business processes as AI-accessible tools through MCP.

#MCP  #ModelContextProtocol  #SAPBTP  #CloudFoundry   #GenerativeAI  #AIAgents  #SAPDevelopers  #OData

entry.title: Understanding Form Templates in SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2
entry.content:
Understanding Output Management in SAP Sales and Service Cloud: Main Templates, Form Templates and Rules

Introduction

Document output is an important part of many business processes in SAP Sales and Service Cloud. Business documents such as invoices, sales documents, service documents, and other forms may need to be generated as PDFs, printed, emailed, or sent to business partners.

SAP provides Output Management capabilities to control how these documents are generated and formatted.

In this blog, we will look at the key concepts involved in Output Management:

  • Form Main Templates
  • Form Templates
  • Language Variants
  • Form Template Rules
  • Adobe LiveCycle Designer

  • How the system determines which template to use

Understanding the relationship between these components is important when implementing customer-specific document layouts.

1. What is Output Management?

Output Management comprises the activities required to generate and distribute business documents.

Form-based documents can be generated:

  • On an ad hoc basis
  • As part of a business process
  • As PDF documents
  • As email attachments
  • For printing
  • For faxing, where supported

The overall output process can be understood using three important components:

Main Template → Form Template → Form Template Rule

The Main Template provides common branding and organizational information.

The Form Template defines the actual document structure and content.

The Form Template Rule determines which form template should be used for a particular business document and under which conditions.

 

2. Form Main Templates

A Form Main Template is used to define common elements that can be reused across multiple form templates.

For example, a company may want the same:

  • Company logo
  • Header
  • Sender address
  • Footer
  • Language-dependent footer

across Quotes , opp, and other business forms.

Instead of maintaining these elements separately in every form, you can maintain them centrally in a Main Template.

 

3. How Does the System Determine the Main Template?

When a business document is generated, the system follows a hierarchy to determine which Main Template should be used.

The basic logic is:

Business Document → Company/Org Unit → Parent Org Unit → Default Main Template

Step 1: Check the assigned organizational unit

The system first checks whether a Main Template is assigned to the company or organizational unit where the business document was created.

The system first searches for a Main Template assigned to Sales US West Coast.

Step 2: Search higher in the organizational structure

If no matching Main Template is found, the system searches upward through the organizational hierarchy.

Step 3: Use the default Main Template

If no matching Main Template is found anywhere in the organizational hierarchy, the system uses the default Main Template.

This allows organizations to have both global and company-specific branding.

 

 

4. Creating a Main Template

To create a Main Template, navigate to:

User Menu → System Settings → All Settings → Output Management → Maintain Main Template

Choose Create.

Enter:

  • Main Template Name

  • Organizational Unit, if applicable

You can also enable the Is Default option if the template should be used as the default.

 

Designing the Main Template

The Main Template provides options for defining the common header and footer information.

Header

You can:

  • Upload a company logo
  • Adjust logo size and alignment
  • Enable a header divider
  • Maintain the sender address

Supported logo formats include:

  • .gif
  • .bmp
  • .jpg
  • .png
  • .tif

The logo should be within the supported size limits. If the uploaded graphic exceeds the supported dimensions, the system automatically resizes it.

Footer

You can configure the number of footer columns and maintain footer information.

Up to four footer blocks can be maintained, with a maximum of 10 lines per footer.

The footer blocks are divided equally across the available space.

 

5. Form Templates

While the Main Template provides common branding elements, the Form Template defines the actual layout and content of a business document.

Form templates are used to generate print forms, which are generally produced as PDF documents.

These forms can then be:

  • Printed
  • Sent as email attachments
  • Sent to business partners
  • Used as part of business processes

The Main Template can then provide the common company logo, sender address, and footer.

6. SAP-Delivered vs Custom Form Templates

SAP provides predefined form templates for many business scenarios.

Although you can create new templates, SAP recommends using and adapting the templates provided by SAP or partners where possible.

A typical approach is:

SAP-Delivered Template → Copy Template → Customize → Publish → Use in Output Rules

This approach has an important advantage: existing output settings can be reused instead of configuring everything from scratch.

7. Why Should You Copy the SAP Template?

Suppose SAP provides a standard Customer Invoice template.

Instead of creating a completely new form, you can:

  1. Select the SAP-delivered template.
  2. Choose Copy Template.
  3. Enter a custom name and description.
  4. Select the required language.
  5. Enable the Form Main Template option if required.
  6. Save and publish the template.

Your organization can then customize the copied template without directly modifying the SAP-delivered version.

This is particularly useful when SAP delivers a newer version of the standard template.

8. Editing Form Templates with Adobe LiveCycle Designer

For more advanced layout changes, SAP supports downloading the form template and modifying it using Adobe LiveCycle Designer.

The required environment includes Adobe LiveCycle Designer along with the relevant SAP support components.

Navigate to:

User Menu → System Settings → All Settings → Output Management → Maintain Form Template

Select the required template and choose Edit.

Depending on the scenario, you can download the template and modify the .xdp file using Adobe LiveCycle Designer.

 

9. What Can Be Changed in Adobe LiveCycle Designer?

Using Adobe LiveCycle Designer, you can make several layout and formatting changes.

For example:

Layout

You can:

  • Change the position of fields
  • Change the position of the title
  • Change the position of the logo
  • Change field alignment
  • Change the sequence of fields

Formatting

You can:

  • Change fonts
  • Change font sizes
  • Change line styles
  • Add borders
  • Change alignment

Fields and Columns

You can:

  • Show or hide fields
  • Change field labels
  • Change column order
  • Change column headers
  • Show or hide columns

However, if a required field is not available in the form data structure, additional extensibility or SAP support may be required.

10. Language Variants

A business may operate across multiple countries and languages.

For example:

  • English
  • German
  • French
  • Spanish

SAP supports language variants of form templates.

A language variant is essentially a version of an existing form template maintained for another language.

To create one:

User Menu → System Settings → All Settings → Output Management → Maintain Form Template

Select the required template and choose:

Copy Variant

Then select the required language.

11. Downloading Form Template Variants

A form template variant can also be downloaded for offline editing or testing.

Navigate to:

User Menu → Settings → All Settings → Output Management → Maintain Form Template

Select the required template and choose Download.

The downloaded ZIP package can contain:

  • XDP file
  • XSD file
  • Sample XML data, if available

The XDP contains the form template definition.

The XSD describes the XML data structure and is useful when editing the form offline.

Sample XML data can be used to preview the output.

If sample data is not available, XML data can also be obtained from the document's output history where supported.

12. Form Template Rules

Now we come to one of the most important parts of Output Management:

Form Template Rules

Imagine you have two invoice templates:

Template A

  • Domestic Quote

Template B

  • International Quote

How does the system know which template to use?

This is where a Form Template Rule is required.

A Form Template Rule defines the conditions under which a particular form template should be selected.

 

13. Main Template + Form Template + Rule: Putting Everything Together

The complete flow can be visualized as:

Business Transaction

↓

Output Management

↓

Form Template Rule

↓

Select Form Template

↓

Apply Main Template

↓

Generate PDF

↓

Print / Email / Other Output Channel

14. Key Takeaways

Here are the key concepts to remember:

1. Main Template

Used for common branding such as:

Logo + Header + Sender Address + Footer

2. Form Template

Defines the actual business document layout and content.

3. Language Variant

Provides the same form in another language.

4. Form Template Rule

Determines which form template should be selected based on defined conditions.

5. Rule Sequence

Specific rules should generally be evaluated before generic rules.

6. SAP-Delivered Templates

Where possible, copy and adapt SAP-delivered templates rather than creating everything from scratch.

7. Adobe LiveCycle Designer

Can be used for advanced layout and form customization where supported.

 

Conclusion

SAP Output Management provides a structured way to manage business document output without having to maintain every document independently.

The most important relationship to understand is:

  • Main Template → Common Branding
  • Form Template → Document Layout and Content
  • Form Template Rule → Template Selection Logic

Once these three concepts are understood, scenarios such as country-specific invoices, company-specific branding, multilingual forms, and different document layouts become easier to configure and manage.

For administrators and implementation teams, paying particular attention to template inheritance, language variants, rule conditions, and rule sequence can help avoid unexpected document output and simplify long-term form maintenance.

entry.title: 7,000 service specialists on one platform: What SAP IT Learned Scaling Enterprise Service Management
entry.content:
Yesterday, at SAP Connect, my colleague Natalia Emelianova - head of our SAP IT project team, shared the story and learnings of SAP's ESM global deployment to date. The transformation and approach are powerful and I want to share my perspective and key points from the session. 

The setup

Running shared services at enterprise scale is genuinely hard. With 110,000+ employees, 500,000+ customers, and operations spanning 157 countries, the complexity behind the scenes compounds quietly, year over year, until the tools you built for one version of the business are struggling to keep up with the next.

What it means at the business level

For operations, HR, and finance leaders, shared services has always been a lever for margin improvement. What we've seen as we've moved to SAP Enterprise Service Management is that when the platform is right, the efficiency gains tend to emerge across several dimensions at once: cycle times compress, cases resolve on first contact more often, and the volume of work that requires specialist intervention starts to shrink.

A 22-42% reduction in case cycle time and increased case deflection for HR services are meaningful indicators, but perhaps more telling is the 85% customer satisfaction score across the platform. When people find it easier to get what they need, the numbers tend to follow.

The ERP integration advantage

One of the things we've found most valuable, and something partners in this space understand well, is how much the native integration with the broader SAP landscape changes what's possible. Running ESM connected to SAP Business Suite, SAP Business AI, SAP Analytics Cloud, and Signavio-based process intelligence means the service layer is working from the same data that drives the business, rather than operating alongside it.

In SAP's Global Finance team, that's already translating into meaningful change across Order-to-Cash, Cash Collection, and Procurement processes. And as autonomous assistants come online for recurring receivables and dispute resolution, the integration becomes even more central allowing an AI-driven action to be grounded in real transaction context, not just a ticket summary.

The everyday experience

Beyond the business case, the more immediate impact is on the people doing the work every day. A finance team processing over 700,000 supplier invoices annually, or an HR organization managing 500,000 support tickets a year, experiences ESM differently than an executive reviewing a quarterly dashboard.

What we hear most from teams on the platform is that the work feels more manageable. Not only are the volume of cases reduced, but the cases that do come through are more complete. They arrive with context already gathered, routing is more accurate, and the tools they're using feel built for the complexity they're actually dealing with. That shift in day-to-day experience is harder to quantify but, in our view, equally important to the efficiency metrics.

Three starting points worth considering

For partners supporting customers through ESM implementations, and for organizations exploring what this kind of transformation could look like, these are the three principles that made the most difference in our own journey:

Process before platform. The technology is ready, but automating a process that isn't well-designed first tends to accelerate the wrong outcomes. Taking time to separate cases from service requests and redesign workflows before going live is where the real foundation gets built.

One line of business proves the model. Starting where the business pain is highest and stakeholder readiness is strongest creates a success story the rest of the organization can see. A phased approach isn't a slower path — it's a more reliable one.

Organizational change management is the implementation. User adoption is ultimately what determines whether the investment delivers. Teams that budget for OCM at the same level as the technical deployment consistently see better outcomes from the start.

In closing

We're grateful to everyone who joined the session and for the conversations that followed. The journey we shared is still in progress, and some of the most valuable thinking we've taken away from SAP Connect has come from partners and customers who are navigating similar challenges in their own organizations.

If you're working through any of these questions — whether you're early in an ESM evaluation or already mid-deployment — we'd genuinely welcome the conversation.

Thank you, @NataliaEmelianova, for providing your insights and delivering such a powerful session!
